main.title: Hitman: Blood Money
main.summary: Hitman: Blood Money is a 2006 stealth video game developed by IO Interactive and published by Eidos Interactive.

cards.heading: Agent 47 faces the Franchise
cards.text: Hitman: Blood Money is a 2006 stealth video game developed by IO Interactive and published by Eidos Interactive. It was released in May 2006 for Microsoft Windows, PlayStation 2, Xbox and Xbox 360. It is the fourth installment in the Hitman video game series, and the sequel to 2004's Hitman: Contracts. The story follows cloned assassin Agent 47's efforts to bring down the Franchise, a rival contract killing organization that is threatening his employers, the International Contract Agency (ICA), and seeking to obtain the same cloning technology that created 47. Meanwhile, a frame story presents 47's life and various contracts he carried out, as narrated by a former FBI director to a journalist.

cards.heading: Reception and later editions
cards.text: Blood Money received critical acclaim for its graphics, narrative, gameplay, voice acting and darker tone; it was also a commercial success, selling more than 2.1 million copies. It has gained a cult following and is considered one of the greatest video games ever made. High-definition ports of Blood Money and two of its predecessors, Hitman 2: Silent Assassin and Contracts, were released on PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 in January 2013 as the Hitman HD Trilogy. A sequel, Hitman: Absolution, was released in 2012, and 4K remastered ports of both Blood Money and Absolution were released by Warner Bros. Interactive Entertainment in 2019 on the PlayStation 4 and Xbox One as part of the Hitman HD Enhanced Collection.

main.title: Time Crisis 4
main.subtitle: A pedal between cover and gunfire
main.summary: Time Crisis 4 combines light-gun shooting with a cover pedal, adding encounters that demand attention in several directions.

cards.heading: Time Crisis 4 Keeps the Light-Gun Shooter Alive Through Cover and Pressure
cards.text: Namco released Time Crisis 4 in Japanese arcades on June 20, 2006. Pressing the pedal brings the player out of cover to fire; releasing it ducks back to safety. Enemies can attack from several directions, so choosing when and where to expose yourself is as important as aiming. The cabinet gives this routine a physical rhythm through the gun and pedal.

cards.heading: GunCon 3 and the PlayStation 3 version
cards.text: The PlayStation 3 edition came with the GunCon 3, compatible with standard and high-definition televisions. Alongside arcade mode, it included a first-person shooter mode with manual movement and gun aiming. Time Crisis 4 later appeared in the 2010 compilation Time Crisis: Razing Storm with PlayStation Move support, though that release omitted the additional first-person mode.

cards.heading: Defending several screens with an infrared light gun
cards.text: Some encounters place the player in a defensive position surrounded by several views. Pointing beyond the edge of the screen changes the direction being watched. The arcade gun uses infrared emitters, replacing the earlier system based on cathode-ray display timing. Players can adjust calibration and switch the gun's blowback effect on or off; standard and deluxe twin cabinets support two players.

cards.heading: Different weapons and defensive encounters
cards.text: The pistol, machine gun, shotgun and grenade launcher return from Time Crisis 3. Vehicle sequences and defensive encounters change the targets: a sniper rifle can disable a truck by shooting its tires, while other scenes require a position to be held. William Rush sometimes appears in the line of fire, forcing players to distinguish an ally from approaching enemies. Voice guidance helps direct attention during these sequences.

main.title: LocoRoco
main.subtitle: Tilt the planet, gather the chorus
main.summary: Japan Studio turned the PSP’s shoulder buttons into a way to tilt a colourful world, guiding soft creatures whose growing numbers bring their songs to life.

cards.heading: A planet moved by the PSP’s shoulder buttons
cards.text: LocoRoco reached European PSPs on 23 June 2006. Developed by Japan Studio and directed by Tsutomu Kouno, it puts the player in control of the planet rather than its inhabitants. The shoulder buttons tilt the landscape, sending its round, soft creatures rolling; using both buttons makes them jump. The aim is to guide them through a colourful world threatened by the Moja Troop.

cards.heading: One rolling creature becomes a crowd
cards.text: Eating berries makes a LocoRoco grow, up to a group of twenty. Pressing ○ splits the large creature into smaller individuals that can squeeze through narrow passages; holding the button brings them together again. Hazards and the Moja can reduce the group, while losing every LocoRoco ends the attempt. Hidden inhabitants, collectibles and completion times give players reasons to explore each stage again.

cards.heading: A train sketch becomes a soft, flat world
cards.text: Kouno’s early idea took shape in a drawing made on a PDA during a train journey: a crowd of round creatures moving and reacting without direct control. A working prototype finally made the concept convincing enough to enter production. Art director Keigo Tsuchiya helped develop a flat, soft-looking visual style, while the two-dimensional presentation kept the creatures’ faces and reactions visible to the player.

cards.heading: A chorus that grows with the LocoRoco
cards.text: Nobuyuki Shimizu and Kemmei Adachi created the music, with lyrics in an invented language devised by Kouno. As more LocoRoco join the group, more voices enter the chorus. The vocal parts play together, with unused layers muted until they are needed, so the song grows without restarting. The creatures’ mouths follow the sound, connecting their expressions, their numbers and the music into one responsive performance.

main.title: Chromehounds
main.subtitle: Build a machine for a particular job
main.summary: Chromehounds is FromSoftware's Xbox 360 mecha combat game, first released in Japan on 29 June 2006. Custom-built HOUNDs fight over Neroimus, an imagined region near the Black Sea. The player assembles a machine whose parts and role affect how it contributes to a battle. The central idea extends beyond winning a duel: a useful HOUND belongs to a group with different responsibilities. Single-player missions introduce those roles, while the original online campaign placed the machines inside a persistent war whose larger direction depended on the competing players and their squads.

cards.text: Chromehounds is FromSoftware's Xbox 360 mecha combat game, first released in Japan on 29 June 2006. Custom-built HOUNDs fight over Neroimus, an imagined region near the Black Sea. The player assembles a machine whose parts and role affect how it contributes to a battle. The central idea extends beyond winning a duel: a useful HOUND belongs to a group with different responsibilities. Single-player missions introduce those roles, while the original online campaign placed the machines inside a persistent war whose larger direction depended on the competing players and their squads.

cards.heading: A squad needs more than one kind of strength
cards.text: Six Role Types provide different ways to participate, from direct combat to support and command responsibilities. The player learns what a machine should accomplish before deciding which equipment makes that possible. Its speed, weapons and arrangement of parts shape the immediate experience of crossing a battlefield. Team planning then connects those individual designs. A powerful gun is useful only if the HOUND carrying it can reach the right place and work with the rest of the squad. Customisation becomes a practical conversation about what the group still needs.

cards.heading: A war whose online life was brief
cards.text: The offline campaign takes place before the Neroimus War, while online play originally presented the conflict itself. Takuji Yoshida directed the game, Toshifumi Nabeshima produced it and Kota Hoshino composed the music. Sega handled its international release in July 2006. The official online servers closed in January 2010, ending the persistent campaign that had supplied much of its identity. Chromehounds remains an unusual experiment in giving a custom machine a social role, where the garage's decisions become meaningful through cooperation with people whose designs can do something different.

main.title: Prey
main.summary: Prey is a 2006 first-person shooter game developed by Human Head Studios, under contract for 3D Realms, and published by 2K Games, while the Xbox 360 version was ported by Venom Games.

cards.text: Prey is a 2006 first-person shooter game developed by Human Head Studios, under contract for 3D Realms, and published by 2K Games, while the Xbox 360 version was ported by Venom Games. The game was initially released in North America and Europe on July 11, 2006. Prey uses a heavily modified version of id Tech 4 to use portals and variable gravity to create the environments the player explores.

The game's story is focused on Cherokee Domasi "Tommy" Tawodi as he, his girlfriend, and grandfather are abducted aboard an alien spaceship known as The Sphere as it consumes material, both inanimate and living, from Earth in order to sustain itself. Tommy's Cherokee heritage allows him to let his spirit roam freely at times and resurrect, giving Tommy an edge in his battle against the Sphere.

Prey had been in development in one form or another since 1995, and has had several major revisions. While the general approach to gameplay, including the use of portals, remained in the game, the story and setting changed several times. The game received generally positive reviews, with critics praising its graphics and gameplay but criticizing its multiplayer component for a lack of content.

Prey was a commercial success, selling more than one million copies in the first two months of its release and leading to the abortive development of its sequel Prey 2. The rights to Prey passed on to Bethesda Softworks, who released a game of the same name, developed by Arkane Studios, in 2017.

main.title: Persona 3
main.summary: Persona 3, released outside Japan as Shin Megami Tensei: Persona 3, is a 2006 role-playing video game developed by Atlus.

cards.text: Atlus released Persona 3 for PlayStation 2 in Japan in 2006. A school year structures this role-playing game: the protagonist attends classes and builds relationships by day, then joins a group of students investigating the Dark Hour. Later editions expanded the original with an epilogue and alternative ways to experience the story.

In Persona 3, the player assumes the role of a high school student who joins the "Specialized Extracurricular Execution Squad" (SEES), a group of students investigating a temporal anomaly known as the "Dark Hour", during which its members can enter Tartarus, a tower containing monsters called Shadows. They battle the Shadows using a physical manifestation of their psyche called a Persona, which they summon by firing a gun-like object called an "Evoker" at their head. Persona 3 incorporates elements of role-playing and simulation games, as the game's protagonist progresses day by day through a school year and forms relationships that improve their Personas' strength in battle.

Critics welcomed the social elements, although some found the battles and environments repetitive. Persona 3 FES added an epilogue that continued the story but omitted the school-life simulation. The game also led to animated films, a manga, concerts and appearances in later Persona spin-offs.

main.title: Rhythm Tengoku
main.subtitle: Listen first and let the action follow
main.summary: Rhythm Tengoku is Nintendo's Game Boy Advance rhythm game built from short, unusual activities whose timing is communicated through music and sound. Created with musician and producer Tsunku, it places a simple action inside a succession of comic situations, asking the player to recognise the beat and respond consistently. The presentation gives each activity a small character of its own, while the controls remain approachable. Released in Japan late in the handheld's life, it established the approach that later reached a wider audience through the Rhythm Heaven series on other Nintendo systems.

cards.heading: Listen first and let the action follow
cards.text: Rhythm Tengoku is Nintendo's Game Boy Advance rhythm game built from short, unusual activities whose timing is communicated through music and sound. Created with musician and producer Tsunku, it places a simple action inside a succession of comic situations, asking the player to recognise the beat and respond consistently. The presentation gives each activity a small character of its own, while the controls remain approachable. Released in Japan late in the handheld's life, it established the approach that later reached a wider audience through the Rhythm Heaven series on other Nintendo systems.

cards.heading: A sound can tell the player when to act
cards.text: Stages emphasise audio cues rather than requiring every input to be read from a scrolling stream of symbols. The player learns a small routine, listens for its timing and performs the action in relation to the music. A change in the sound can announce a different response, making attention to the rhythm more useful than simply watching the character move. The system allows a straightforward control to support many kinds of activity. What must be learned is the relationship between the heard cue and the moment when the response belongs.

cards.heading: A simple routine becomes a performance
cards.text: Reaching the end of an activity produces an assessment of the player's timing, encouraging another attempt with a more reliable sense of its rhythm. The comic art gives a missed beat an immediate visible consequence, while the music keeps the routine coherent even when the situation is unusual. Rhythm Tengoku makes improvement easy to recognise through the difference between merely finishing an activity and performing it smoothly. Its collection grows around that repeated pleasure, allowing the player to learn another small task without losing the common skill of listening carefully before acting.

main.title: Star Fox Command
main.summary: Fox McCloud's DS adventure joins stylus-controlled dogfights to a tactical map, where drawn flight paths determine who fights and what happens to the Great Fox.

cards.heading: The game
cards.text: Star Fox Command is a space-combat and strategy game developed by Nintendo and Q-Games for Nintendo DS. Released first in Japan in 2006, it brings Fox McCloud and his allies to the handheld with stylus-controlled flight, tactical route planning and a branching story.

cards.heading: Draw the next move
cards.text: With the Star Fox team scattered and the Anglar army threatening the Lylat system, Fox must bring his allies back into the fight. Command gives the player a tactical map before sending them into the cockpit. Drawing a line from each fighter sets its route for the turn; crossing an enemy's path starts a battle. Fuel limits how far a ship can travel, and hostile forces keep moving towards the Great Fox. Choosing an interception therefore also means deciding who stays close enough to defend the mothership.

cards.heading: Fly by touch
cards.text: The stylus has a second job once combat begins. Sliding it across the touch screen steers the fighter, double taps control boosting or braking, and quick strokes trigger a roll. The upper screen shows the dogfight while the lower screen provides radar and manoeuvre controls. Destroying marked enemies and collecting their cores clears an encounter before the fuel timer expires. Bombs can be directed to a position on the radar, making the lower screen a practical part of the attack rather than simply a display to glance at.

cards.heading: Different pilots, different futures
cards.text: Each pilot brings a fighter with its own laser, lock-on pattern, shields and boost capacity. Those differences matter when assigning encounters on the map, especially as several pilots move during the same turn. The story also changes with decisions between missions: its branches lead to nine endings and different futures for Fox and his companions. Returning to a junction can therefore reveal another side of a character as well as another battle. In the gallery, each pilot's profile has a musical theme, giving the expanded cast its own sound.

main.title: Ultimate Ghosts 'n Goblins
main.subtitle: Arthur returns to another hostile kingdom
main.summary: Ultimate Ghosts 'n Goblins is Tose and Capcom's PSP action-platform game, first released in Japan on 3 August 2006. Arthur again fights through demons and traps, with three-dimensional scenery surrounding a largely side-on route. Series creator Tokuro Fujiwara returned to lead the project. The familiar image remains a knight whose armour can disappear after an encounter goes wrong, leaving him vulnerable in his underwear. New systems change how that danger is managed, giving the handheld game another way to balance the series' demanding action with a longer journey through its stages.

cards.heading: Arthur returns to another hostile kingdom
cards.text: Ultimate Ghosts 'n Goblins is Tose and Capcom's PSP action-platform game, first released in Japan on 3 August 2006. Arthur again fights through demons and traps, with three-dimensional scenery surrounding a largely side-on route. Series creator Tokuro Fujiwara returned to lead the project. The familiar image remains a knight whose armour can disappear after an encounter goes wrong, leaving him vulnerable in his underwear. New systems change how that danger is managed, giving the handheld game another way to balance the series' demanding action with a longer journey through its stages.

cards.heading: Survive the mistake, then decide where to search
cards.text: Standard mode gives Arthur several lives and allows revival at the point of defeat while those lives remain. Improved armour can also withstand more than one hit, changing the immediate cost of an error. The player still has to read enemy movement and commit to jumps carefully, because losing the last protection makes the next contact dangerous. Different weapons and abilities provide alternatives, while exploration gives reasons to look beyond the most direct path. The new allowances make room to learn a hostile section without removing the need to understand why it defeated Arthur.

cards.heading: A creator revisits a demanding formula
cards.text: Fujiwara's return connects the PSP release to the series' early arcade identity while the new presentation brings its monsters and environments into three dimensions. Masaya Tsunemoto and Kazuhiro Kotani supplied the music. North American and European editions followed shortly after Japan in 2006. The game is a new chapter rather than a simple transfer of an older release, changing survival rules and adding ways to explore. Its central appeal remains the same difficult bargain: Arthur is capable enough to win, but the player must learn to use that capability in places designed to punish carelessness.

main.title: Saints Row
main.subtitle: A new recruit claims a place in Stilwater
main.summary: Saints Row is Volition's Xbox 360 open-world action game, first released in North America on 29 August 2006. A player-created character joins the 3rd Street Saints after the gang saves their life, then helps it challenge rival organisations across Stilwater. The city can be explored on foot or by vehicle, with story missions and smaller activities drawing the player into its districts. The campaign is divided between opposing gangs rather than one uninterrupted chain of assignments. Building a reputation becomes the means of deciding which part of that struggle to pursue next.

cards.heading: A new recruit claims a place in Stilwater
cards.text: Saints Row is Volition's Xbox 360 open-world action game, first released in North America on 29 August 2006. A player-created character joins the 3rd Street Saints after the gang saves their life, then helps it challenge rival organisations across Stilwater. The city can be explored on foot or by vehicle, with story missions and smaller activities drawing the player into its districts. The campaign is divided between opposing gangs rather than one uninterrupted chain of assignments. Building a reputation becomes the means of deciding which part of that struggle to pursue next.

cards.heading: Earn the right to take the next job
cards.text: Activities and side missions award Respect, which is spent to unlock story missions. The system makes the city's diversions part of the campaign's progress rather than leaving them entirely outside it. Driving, shooting and calling on gang allies provide familiar tools for dealing with the work that follows. Customising the protagonist helps make the rise through the Saints feel like the player's own career. Stilwater becomes useful through repeated visits, as a district contains both the next conflict and an activity that can supply the standing needed to begin it.

cards.heading: The first shape of a changing series
cards.text: Steve Jaros wrote the story for a project published by THQ. Reviews were positive, often comparing its open-world design favourably with Grand Theft Auto, and sales passed one million copies by the end of 2006. Online multiplayer added cooperative and competitive activities beyond the single-player city. Its success led to Saints Row 2 in 2008 and a franchise that would become increasingly extravagant. The original remains a more grounded introduction to the Saints, establishing the created protagonist, rival gangs and expandable city that gave the later games their starting point.
